subtitle: Write Django views that read what the client sent and answer with JSON and the right status code.
notes: This deck goes with exercise 2. By the end you should be able to write a view that reads a query or a JSON body, checks it, and replies with JSON and a fitting status code.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.text:
In exercise 1 you split a raw request by hand. Django does that for you, then **calls a function you wrote** and passes the request in. That function is a **view**.

A view is like a clerk at a counter: take the form, check it, hand back a reply slip with a stamp on top: "OK", "filled in wrong" or "wrong counter". The stamp is the **status code**.
slides.notes: Link to data work: before you do maths on a column, you check it exists and holds numbers. A view does the same with what the client sent.

slides.title: What the tests send
slides.caption: You don't build `request` yourself: the tests make a fake one and call your view with it.
slides.code:
factory = RequestFactory()

greet(factory.get("/greet/", {"name": "Ada"}))   # like GET /greet/?name=Ada

add(factory.post("/add/", data='{"a": 2, "b": 3.5}',
                 content_type="application/json"))   # a POST with a JSON body
slides.notes: RequestFactory makes request objects without running a server. Inside greet, request is a GET whose query has name set to Ada. Inside add, the body is the text {"a": 2, "b": 3.5}.

slides.title: What your views must return
slides.caption: The tests check the status code and the JSON. Error messages must match exactly.
slides.notes: A name of only spaces also gets the 400. For add, {"a": 1} (b missing) and {"a": null, "b": 2} get the same 'must be numbers' error. null is JSON's way of writing None.

slides.title: New words

terms.meaning: A function that receives a request and returns a response.
Text data that looks like a dict: `{"message": "Hello"}`.
`200` OK, `400` client sent something wrong, `405` wrong method.
Values in the address after `?` / data sent inside the request.
An `@` line just above `def` that adds behaviour.

slides.notes: Codes starting with 4 mean the client made a mistake. Codes starting with 5 mean the server broke. A user's typo should never cause a 500.

slides.title: Tool: request.GET.get
slides.caption: `request.GET` holds the query. `.get(name, default)` gives the default instead of crashing.
slides.code:
request = RequestFactory().get("/weather/", {"city": "  Paris  "})
print(request.method)
print(request.GET.get("city", ""))
print(request.GET.get("country", "unknown"))
print(request.GET.get("city", "").strip())
slides.notes: request.GET["city"] with square brackets crashes when the parameter is missing. The value is always text, so .strip() works on it.

slides.title: Tool: JsonResponse
slides.caption: A class you call like a function. The status is 200 unless you pass `status=`.
slides.code:
response = JsonResponse({"error": "city is required"}, status=400)
print(response.status_code)
print(response.content)
print(JsonResponse({"temp": 21}).status_code)
slides.notes: The b'...' means bytes: raw text ready to send over the network. You don't need to do anything with it.

slides.title: Tool: @require_POST and @require_GET
slides.caption: Write it on the line directly above `def`. A wrong method gets a 405 and your code never runs.
slides.notes: No brackets: @require_GET, not @require_GET(). The Console also logs 'Method Not Allowed (GET): /ping/'. That's Django noting the 405, not a bug.

slides.title: Tools: json.loads and try / except
slides.code:
body = b'{"item": "tea", "qty": 2}'     # what request.body looks like
data = json.loads(body)
print(data["qty"] * 10)
print(data.get("price"))

try:
    json.loads("{oops")
except json.JSONDecodeError:
    print("That was not valid JSON")
slides.output:
20
None
That was not valid JSON
slides.notes: json.loads is a function: it turns JSON text or bytes into Python. Broken JSON raises an error, which would be a 500. try / except catches it so you can reply with a polite 400 instead.

slides.title: Query vs body
slides.notes: request.POST is a trap: it only holds HTML form data, not JSON. For JSON, always use json.loads(request.body).

slides.title: Pattern: check, then use
slides.caption: The same shape you need in `add`, on different data (just the logic, not a view):
slides.output: width and height must be numbers
slides.notes: isinstance(value, (int, float)) asks 'is it any of these types?'. The text "3" and None both give False. Use or: the error is needed if either value is bad.

slides.title: Your task, step by step

steps.text: If the name is empty, return the error with `status=400`
If `a` or `b` is not an int or float, return a 400

slides.notes: Steps 1-4 are greet, steps 5-8 are add. if not name: catches both a missing name and one made only of spaces, because an empty string counts as false.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Error dict without `status=400`: the JSON looks right, the status is 200
`request.POST` for JSON: it only holds form data; use `request.body`
`if a and b:` isn't a number check: `"1"` is true, `0` is false
`and` instead of `or`: the error is needed if **either** value is bad
A typo like `"Name is required"`: the tests compare text exactly

slides.title: Where you'll use this
slides.text: A shop's mobile app sends `POST /api/cart/` with `{"item": 42, "qty": "two"}`. Your view must spot the bad quantity and reply **400** with a clear message, not crash with a **500**.
bullets: Every Django API endpoint is a view: read, validate, return JSON and a status
The app shows your error message to the user, so it must be clear
Django REST Framework later does the parsing and checking for you, in the same pattern

slides.title: Check yourself
questions: What does `request.GET.get("name", "")` give when the name is missing?
Which status fits a missing name: 200, 400, 405 or 500? Why?
Where is a JSON body in a plain Django view, and how do you read it?
Why is `isinstance(value, (int, float))` safer than `if value:`?
